script: CEO tried to short me— I exposed betrayal, stole back, never caught.. A year out of school in the early‑1990s, I landed a job as a business analyst at this massive family‑owned tech firm in Silicon Valley. The company was booming, cash‑flow was insane, and the family's net worth was in the high‑9/low‑10‑figure range. They were neurotic, moody, and always hungry for more money—no wonder they never hit the household‑name level. I climbed the ladder fast. I got to sit in the same room as the owners and worked on projects that paid off big. I started talking to them about my tech stock gains, just as a casual chat—nothing official. Then, late 1999, one of the owners pulls me aside and says, "I want you to invest my personal money. Throw a million at high‑risk plays and see what happens." I was like, "Sure, but let's put it in writing." I got a signed deal: 20% of any profit from this side hustle, and a note that this was a personal deal, not part of my job. I had been watching the market and spotting weak tech firms that were over‑valued. I knew they'd crash. So right after the 2000 New Year, I used both my cash and the owner's cash to short tech stocks. I kept the accounts separate, but both were under my name. I documented everything and got the owner's consent. In the first two months, both accounts lost some money, but the bubble burst and the owner's account shot up like crazy. Fast forward to June. The company's revenue dipped, but we were still profitable. The owner, clueless about my strategy, asks me how his money is doing. I tell him we're still holding options and shorts, and that we just closed some trades that netted $1.35 million in cash in his account. I say, "I'll wire you the $280,000, but I am taking my 20% cut—$70,000—before that." He goes all‑out about how we're all in a tough spot, that I should be grateful for a job, and that the whole $350,000 is needed for the company. I am like, "Bruh, that's not true. We have more upside coming from the open positions." He didn't get it. He kept yelling about the $70,000 and how it was essential. I decided to play the long game. I sent back the entire $1.35 million, left the open positions untouched, and let the market do its thing. He never brought it up again; he thought the money was all there and didn't ask for any audit or records. I kept the extra $1.8 million that came from covering all the shorts and exercising the puts. After three more years, I left the company, paid taxes on the gain, and walked away with a fat nest egg. No one ever questioned it. The irony? While I was doing the dirty work, the owners promoted me, thinking I was loyal for giving them the cash and not fussing over the $70,000. They didn't see I had outsmarted them. The company eventually collapsed over family disputes, but the owners left in good financial shape—if they'd just stopped being shady with everyone, they'd have been a powerhouse. Fast‑forward to 2026. The original firm folded. A younger, cleaner generation revived a similar business, and it's doing pretty well now. I still keep a good relationship with the surviving family members, and I do consulting for them. It's a profitable, harmless partnership. I am just glad no one ever found out the old story.
